title: Le Chatelier's principle
question: What is Le Chatelier's principle?

principle.name: Le Chatelier's principle
principle.formulaNote: Q is the reaction quotient (the mixture as it is now) and K is the equilibrium constant (the mixture at balance). Q always moves to K. Add or remove a substance, squeeze the mixture or heat it, and the reaction shifts in the direction that undoes part of the change. Only temperature changes K itself
principle.idea: Many reactions run both ways and settle at a balance where the forward and backward rates are equal. Disturb that balance and the reaction shifts to undo part of what you did.
principle.discovered: 1884 · Henry Louis Le Chatelier, Paris; found independently by Karl Ferdinand Braun in 1887. It builds on Guldberg and Waage's law of mass action (1864) and van 't Hoff's work on equilibrium and heat (1884)

examples.title: Making ammonia for fertiliser
examples.text: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ turns four gas molecules into two and gives out heat. So plants squeeze the gas to about 200 bar, and run at a compromise 400–450 °C: cooler would give more ammonia, but far too slowly.

examples.title: The recycle loop of a urea plant
examples.text: One pass over the iron catalyst converts only about 15 %. Cooling the gas turns the ammonia liquid and removes it, so the reaction starts forward again. Going round the loop lifts the total to about 97 %. India made about 314 lakh tonnes of urea this way in 2023–24.

examples.title: Opening a fizzy drink
examples.text: A sealed cola holds about 7 g of CO₂ per litre under about 4 bar of gas. Twist the cap, the pressure above drops, and the dissolved gas is suddenly too much for the balance: it bubbles out. A warm bottle loses it faster.

examples.title: Blood picking up oxygen
examples.text: Hb + O₂ ⇌ HbO₂. In the lungs oxygen pressure is about 100 mmHg, so haemoglobin fills to about 98 %. At Leh, 3,500 m up, thinner air leaves it about 90 % full.

examples.title: Blood letting oxygen go
examples.text: A working muscle uses oxygen and makes acid and heat. Low oxygen pressure shifts the balance back, and haemoglobin hands over its oxygen just where it is needed.

examples.title: Scale in a geyser or kettle
examples.text: Hard water holds dissolved limestone only while it also holds CO₂. Heating drives the CO₂ out, the balance tips, and calcium carbonate comes out as a white crust on the hot element.

examples.title: A dishwasher's softener
examples.text: Resin beads swap the calcium in hard water for sodium. When the beads are full, a flush of strong salt water pushes the same exchange backwards and washes the calcium away.

examples.title: Stalactites in a limestone cave
examples.text: Rain soaks up CO₂ in soil and dissolves limestone. When a drop reaches cave air with far less CO₂, the gas escapes and a film of stone is left. Mawmluh cave in Meghalaya grew a record of the last 4,200 years this way.

examples.title: A brown gas that fades when squeezed
examples.text: Colourless N₂O₄ ⇌ 2 brown NO₂. Squeeze the mixture and it shifts towards N₂O₄, the side with fewer molecules. Warm it and it shifts towards NO₂ and turns darker, because splitting takes in heat.

hook: At equilibrium a reaction has not stopped: molecules still split and join, at matching rates. Squeeze, heat or feed a live box of molecules and watch Q walk back to K. Then run a Haber converter at 200 bar, open a fizzy bottle, climb to Leh with your haemoglobin, fur up a kettle and grow a stalactite.

explainer.title: Both ways at once
explainer.text: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ runs forwards and backwards together. The amounts level off where the two rates match, with Q equal to K (0.15 bar at 25 °C). Squeeze the gas and it shifts to fewer molecules; heat it and K itself rises a hundredfold by 100 °C. The shift undoes part of the change, never all of it.

explainer.title: Bread from air
explainer.text: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ gives out heat and halves the number of molecules. At 200 bar the balance holds 38 % ammonia at 400 °C, 27 % at 450 °C and 19 % at 500 °C. Plants accept about 15 % per pass at 400–450 °C over iron, tap off the liquid ammonia and recycle the rest to reach about 97 %.

explainer.title: Fizz and breath
explainer.text: A cola holds about 7 g/L of CO₂ under 4 bar; open it and Q leaps above K, so gas leaves. Haemoglobin is 98 % full at the 100 mmHg of oxygen in your lungs, about 75 % in resting muscle and far less in working muscle. At Leh's 3,500 m it fills to about 90 %.

explainer.title: Scale and caves
explainer.text: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻. Water under open air holds about 50 mg/L of limestone, under CO₂-rich soil air 200 mg/L or more. Boil it and the CO₂ leaves, so scale forms. Drip it into a cave and a stalactite grows, about 0.13 mm a year.

explainer.title: Where the rule slips
explainer.text: A catalyst speeds both directions equally and moves nothing. Argon pumped into a rigid tank moves nothing either, but under a free piston it shifts the balance back. Adding nitrogen to a nitrogen-rich ammonia mix makes more nitrogen. The words can mislead; comparing Q with K never does.

concepts.def: A reaction that can run forwards and backwards, written with the double arrow ⇌.
The state in which forward and backward reactions run at equal rates, so amounts stay steady although molecules keep reacting.
The fixed value the ratio of products to reactants reaches at balance. It changes only with temperature.
The same ratio worked out for the mixture as it is now. If Q is below K the forward reaction wins; above K, the backward one.
Disturb a system at equilibrium and it shifts in the direction that undoes part of the disturbance.
A substance that speeds a reaction without being used up. It speeds both directions equally, so it cannot move the balance.
The amount of gas a liquid holds at balance is proportional to the pressure of that gas above it.
How much product you get compared with the most possible. Equilibrium sets its ceiling; speed decides how close you come.
